newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Bombs kill three in Kabul, wound seven.
newsitem.headline: Bombs kill three in Kabul, wound seven.

text.p: Khan Coco's hands were covered in dust from digging through the remains of a mud-brick house looking for survivors after bombs dropped on Kabul on Thursday killed three of his neighbours and wounded seven.
"They were having breakfast when the bombs landed," said Coco, referring to the family whose home was blasted by two 250 kg (550 lb) bombs in the Deh Kepak district of northwest Kabul.
Forces loyal to the ousted Afghan government dropped a total of five bombs on Kabul during two air raids on Thursday, killing three children and wounding seven people, witnesses said.
The deaths were believed to be the first war-related civilian fatalities in Kabul since the purist Islamic Taleban militia overtook the capital in late September.

The two 250 kg bombs, dropped in the Deh Kepak district at around 8 a.m., caused all the injuries. There are no reports of injuries from the other bombs, which fell close to the airport on the northeastern edge of the city.
The father of two of the dead children, Dr Abdullah, was in serious condition in hospital. His seven-year-old son Hamid and 14-year-old daughter Malina were killed, witnesses said.
In the other house that was hit, the body of the third dead child, seven-year-old Matine, lay on a rope-strung bed covered with the blanket under which he had spent his last night.
Around the charpoy women wailed and Matine's sister stood in shock, a blood-stained bandage around her dust-caked head.

The bombs reduced many of the houses to rubble. Dr Abdullah's neighbours had stretched a tarpaulin from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) over the gaping hole the bomb had blown in the outside wall of the house.
In a small cemetery nearby, graves for the three children were already being dug an hour after the strike. They will be buried among graves of previous war victims.

Local people said they believed the plane was sent by northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, a partner in an alliance fighting the Taleban north of Kabul. They did not know why the bombs had been dropped in that area.
"This is not near a military base, and I don't know why they are bombing people's houses here," said Coco.
International organisations estimate that more than 25,000, and perhaps as many as 50,000 civilians have died in factional fighting in Kabul since a Moscow-backed government was overthrown in 1992.
